notes.short: Nehemiah shakes out his robe to seal an oath
notes.about: The nobles have sworn before the priests to give back what they took from the poor. Nehemiah then shakes out the folds of his robe, and his words give the meaning: so may God shake out of house and goods anyone who breaks the promise. The whole assembly answers “Amen.”

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: I also shook out the folds of my robe
figure.means: a curse on anyone who breaks the oath: as the robe is shaken out and emptied, so may God empty him of his house and goods

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a symbolical action that made the sworn agreement more binding, Nehemiah's words declaring its meaning. Robert Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a solemn and significant gesture calling down a curse on any who broke the oath. Joseph Benson says Nehemiah showed by an outward sign, as the prophets often did, how God would cast out oath-breakers.
notes.limit: Nehemiah acts here as governor, not as a prophet: the act seals the oath the nobles had just sworn.

cites.quote: To make the agreement thus sworn to still more binding, Nehemiah confirmed the proceeding by a symbolical action ... The symbolical action consisted in Nehemiah's gathering up his garment as if for the purpose of carrying something, and then shaking it out with the words above stated, which declared the meaning of the act.

cites.quote: The proceedings were closed by the parties binding themselves by a solemn oath, administered by the priests, that they would redeem their pledge, as well as by the governor invoking, by the solemn and significant gesture of shaking a corner of his garment, a malediction on those who should violate it.

cites.quote: Thus he represented, by an external sign, as the manner of the prophets often was, how God would cast them out of their possessions, and of the fruit of their labours, who did not observe this oath.
